title: Family of Hamilton man shot dead by police hire law firm, private investigator
subtitle: The Special Investigations Unit probe into Erixon Kabera's death is ongoing.
article: The family of Erixon Kabera has hired a law firm and private investigator to probe the fatal police shooting of the father of three.

Made possible by some $50,000 sourced through an ongoing GoFundMe , Yves Ikobe, one of Kabera's younger brothers, said the decision to retain counsel and a PI comes amid a provincial watchdog investigation into the November shooting, which so far has provided few answers.
"We haven't heard anything about what he did wrong to deserve this," Ikobe, 34, said over a call Wednesday.
Kabera, 43, died at 2:47 a.m. Nov. 10 - about nine hours after he was shot by Hamilton police on the fifth-floor hallway of his Main Street West condo building.

Friends and family have been searching for answers ever since, their efforts supported by scores of community members and politicians - about 300 attended a vigil for Kabera on Nov. 14 - who've called for more transparency in the Special Investigations Unit probe.

They say their search was complicated by inaccurate information released in the immediate wake of the shooting, when the SIU, an arm's length agency that probes all police-involved shootings in Ontario, said the incident occurred during an exchange of gunfire.
The SIU later clarified two officers shot Kabera after an "interaction."
Investigators found a replica firearm in the fifth-floor hallway, the SIU previously said, without explaining how it may have been used.

Hamilton police - who can only comment on the lead-up to the incident, not the shooting, due to the SIU probe - said officers were called to the building after a resident reported a man outside her door who she believed had a gun.
It's unclear what exactly happened when police arrived.

Ikobe said records his family obtained from Hamilton General Hospital showed Kabera was admitted with multiple gunshot wounds, including some to his chest, as well as broken bones in his arms. He added it's unclear from the records how the breaks were sustained.
"He was in the operating room for over four hours," the grieving brother added.
Ikobe declined to share the medical records with The Spectator citing advice from the family's recently hired legal team at Falconers LLP, a Toronto-based firm.

The SIU didn't respond to questions over claims Kabera suffered broken bones during the fatal interaction. A spokesperson said via email an autopsy was completed Nov. 11 and there are no updates in the investigation.

Three days after the shooting, Ikobe said he and other family members were allowed to enter the unit where Kabera had lived for the last few years. He saw what he described as bullet holes in the hallway, on the walls leading to Kabera's front door, on the door itself and inside the apartment.
"So much damage," he said. "It was a lot."

The chaotic scene Ikobe likened to being out of a movie makes no sense to the family. The Kabera they knew is kind, a hard worker for the Canada Revenue Agency and a caring father deeply involved in the Rwandan community. His childhood nickname, Gentil, was a testament to those qualities, Ikobe added. Meanwhile, the family never knew him to have guns, including replicas. He also never complained about having issues with a neighbour, nor were they aware of any serious mental health issues.

Ikobe said the suddenness of his brother's death - Kabera was supposed to move to Montreal the day after the shooting to work on a food distribution business with his uncle - has made it all the more difficult to accept.
Kabera came to Canada in 2005 and lived with his wife and three kids in Toronto before coming to Hamilton several years ago.

In both cities, he paid homage to his Rwandan roots, helping newcomers with documentation and volunteering. Locally, his volunteer work included a relationship with Hamilton police, organizing annual events where the two groups got together and played sports.
In recent days, multiple Rwandan organizations have sent letters to Hamilton's police chief demanding accountability while commemorating Kabera's advocacy work.

"As a staunch supporter of our initiatives, he consistently showed up to champion our work," wrote Prime Luminisce Rwanda, a group of Canadian-Rwandan artists based in Toronto, in one such letter, which was also sent to media outlets. "To us, he was not just a community member but a model of excellence and true cultural ambassador."
"It is essential that the investigation is conducted fairly, and justice is served," the Canadian chapter of the organization Rwandan Community Abroad (RCA) wrote in another.
Ikobe echoed those sentiments, saying part of the reason the family has retained a law firm and private investigator is to ensure "the truth comes out."
"Transparency through this investigation is the most important thing we need as a family and a community."
